title: The Moon's Sandy Secret
markdown:
It was a glorious morning by the sea, the sort where the sun winks and the sand tickles. The air hummed with beachcombers and the sigh of waves. Flags for the Sandcastle Jubilee snapped above a row of buckets; somebody had already lost a spade to a hole and was laughing about it. Etta, explorer whose pockets clinked with stones and shells from hidden grottos, was buzzing. Today she, Brim the bat, and Ranger Jo were ready to build a castle that would make the ocean smile — or at least pause before swallowing it.

Brim, wings like dark velvet, a giggle like rustling leaves, flitted around Etta’s head. “A tall tower! Taller than a seagull! And a moat — deep — to keep out busy sea creatures.” Whiskers twitching. Ranger Jo, wide-brimmed hat with a band of pressed wildflowers, smiled and began scooping with a big friendly shovel. Happy shouts, sandy hands. Etta dug foundations that meant to reach the heart of the shore. Brim arranged seashells like jewels. Jo formed sturdy walls against any playful breeze.

Just as Etta placed the last pearly shell on the highest turret, a sneaky wave — not a roar, a tiptoe — crept up. Whoosh. Foamy fingers at the base, a soft sigh, a wet patch where the castle had stood. “My beautiful castle!” Etta’s eyes clouded. Brim fluttered down, cheerful face dented. “My shell bridge!” A charming pathway of polished shells had gone into wet sand.

They tried again, a little further from the water, thinking themselves safe, packing the walls harder, adding a second ring of shells as if decoration could argue with foam. The sea had a hide-and-seek in mind. A quiet lick took the south corner. Another took Brim’s bridge at the exact moment he had finished the last cowrie. Again and again even the gentler waves crept closer, nibbling, until the sand was a lumpy wet mess, completely un-castle-like. Etta sat back on her heels, salty to the elbows, and refused to blame the jubilee.

Etta looked at Jo, brow furrowed. “Why does the sea keep coming so close? Not just the big crashes. The whole ocean moving in and out, slowly, like breathing.”

Brim pointed a tiny claw up, body still. “The sun is high, but the moon is out too. Pale. Definitely there.”

Jo’s eyes twinkled like light on water. She patted the sand. Sit. The water had gone far out, a wide stretch they had not seen before. She drew a circle with her finger. “The ocean is a very big thing, always being pulled. The moon has a tug.”

“A tug? How can a tug be so strong?”

“That tug makes the water come closer. High tide — the ocean stretching its arms. When the tug is weaker, or the moon is on the other side of the world, the water moves back. Low tide.” She gestured at the horizon, more sand revealed. “Lower now. Soon the journey continues and the water comes in again.”

A spark. Not a naughty sea. A loyal pull. “We build when the tug is getting weaker. When the water is going out. Low tide.” Brim nodded, bat-brain quick. “And higher up. A sand hill. Where the tug doesn’t reach as much.”

They began again, this time watching the wet line instead of wishing it away. Jo: a strong wide base on a slightly raised mound, stamped until it sounded dull and sure. As the water crept back they would add height, a shield. Joyful rhythm — scoop, pack, turn. Walls rising. Brim ferried shells only after the corners held. They dug a small clever channel to guide water around the masterpiece, a little river protecting a kingdom, and tested it with a bucket before trusting the tide.

As the moon continued its silent journey and the tide came in, the castle stood. Waves lapped the defenses, whispering to the sand; towers intact, shells gleaming. Built with understanding as well as grit. Brim did a loop-the-loop. Etta beamed at a castle that had learned the moon’s timing.

Jo did not compare trees shedding leaves or invite more wonders. She named the rhythm once: tides. Work with it, not against it.

Etta looked at the shimmering ocean, then at the pale moon painting a silvery path. “The moon really does pull the sea. Like magic, but real.” Brim rested on her shoulder, wings tucked, and left the owl impressions to actual owls. They sat until the channel took the next lazy lick of foam and the jubilee judges, when they came, would find something still standing.
